planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto saturated, mineral-rich soil for natural winter stratification, or install spring plugs; this rhizomatous sedge spreads gradually to form a loose colony rather than staying in a single tuft.

directions: Fen sedge is a slender, rhizome-spreading sedge of calcareous fens, spring-fed seeps, and wet prairie swales, where its fine blue-green foliage knits together with other fen specialists over mineral-charged, constantly moist soil. Unlike tightly tufted fen sedges it often grows alongside, this species creeps gently by short rhizomes to form loose patches rather than single clumps, making it useful for stabilizing the saturated margins of a spring-fed bog garden. It needs year-round moisture and alkaline, mineral-rich soil to persist, and should be sourced only as nursery-propagated plugs or seed given how scarce intact fen habitat has become. Once sited correctly it is essentially maintenance-free and needs no dividing or fertilizing.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto wet-mesic, mineral-rich soil in fall so winter cold-moist conditions release dormancy; the fleshy tuberous roots resist transplanting once established, so pick the permanent site before sowing.

directions: Tuberous Indian plantain is a stout composite of Ozark fens, calcareous wet-mesic prairies, and glade seep margins, identifiable by its cluster of fleshy, tuber-like roots and solid flowering stem, a reliable field mark separating it from the hollow-stemmed prairie Indian plantain it sometimes grows near. Flat-topped heads of small, dull white, faintly fragrant flowers open in mid- to late summer and draw a steady traffic of small bees, wasps, and soldier beetles. Because its swollen roots store energy for a site adapted to fluctuating fen moisture, it tolerates somewhat drier footing than true obligate fen plants, making it a good transition species between a wet seep and the surrounding prairie matrix. Leave the clump undisturbed once planted, since the tuberous root system rarely survives division or relocation.

planting.note: Surface-sow the tiny seed in fall or late winter, since light aids germination; seedlings establish slowly in shallow, rocky, lime-rich soil and resent any organic mulch piled against the crown.

directions: Round-fruit St. John's wort is a low, woody-based perennial of the exposed dolomite and limestone glades of the Missouri Ozarks, where thin, baking-hot soil over bedrock keeps competing vegetation sparse. Clusters of small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers open through early and midsummer, followed by the rounded, globe-shaped seed capsules that give the plant its common name and persist as a textural feature into fall. It thrives on neglect in lean, rocky, well-drained alkaline soil and full sun, declining quickly if given rich garden loam or regular irrigation. Use it at the front of a dry rock garden or glade-style planting alongside other calciphile companions, where its fine-textured foliage and tidy habit need no staking or deadheading.

subcategory: Kansas Flint Hills tallgrass prairie forb

planting.note: Fall-sow onto well-drained, gravelly or clay-loam soil for winter stratification, or set out spring-grown plugs; the long taproot makes bare-root transplanting difficult once plants are past their first year.

directions: Tall cinquefoil is an upright, clump-forming prairie perennial found across the drier upland swales of the Kansas Flint Hills, where its deep taproot lets it keep flowering through the clay-and-limestone soils that stop many shallower-rooted forbs. Crowded clusters of small, cream-white, strawberry-like flowers open from early summer into fall atop downy, dark green compound foliage, drawing a steady run of small native bees and syrphid flies. It is one of the quieter companion species that fills gaps between big bluestem and indiangrass tussocks without competing aggressively for root space, and it handles drought, fire, and mowing once its first-year taproot is established. Give it lean to average, sharply drained soil in full sun and skip supplemental watering after the first season.

subcategory: Kansas Flint Hills tallgrass prairie forb

planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly onto undisturbed upland prairie soil, since cold winter moisture is needed to break dormancy; the thick taproot makes this species far better suited to direct seeding than transplanting.

directions: Prairie false dandelion is a low, taprooted perennial of unplowed Flint Hills upland prairie, sending up solitary, dandelion-like yellow flower heads on short, leafless stalks in April and May before the surrounding big bluestem and little bluestem have greened up for the season. Its narrow, wavy-edged basal leaves stay close to the ground year-round, letting it dodge competition from taller warm-season grasses that dominate by midsummer. Because its presence generally signals old, undisturbed prairie sod, it is slow to colonize and best used in a dedicated native seed mix for a prairie restoration or meadow planting rather than a conventional bed. It needs lean, well-drained soil and full sun, and once established requires no irrigation or care beyond periodic fire or mowing to control taller competitors.
